intro: Adjectives describe people and things. Use a comparative for two; use a superlative for one in a group of three or more.
scopeNote: Core rules match the experiments. Extra reading covers more textbook patterns.
sourceNote: Based on teacher-provided Chapter 6, pages 32–35, with simplified explanations and original examples.

sections.title: Comparatives and superlatives
sections.text: Use than to introduce the other item: taller than. We usually use the in superlative patterns: the tallest.
examples: Ming is taller than Ben.
Ming is the tallest in our class.
sections.note: In these Lab answers, include than for comparatives and the for superlatives.

sections.title: Short-word forms
sections.text: Many short adjectives add -er/-est. Words ending in e add -r/-st. For words like happy, remove y before -ier/-iest. For big and fat, double the final consonant.
examples: Our kitchen is bigger than our bathroom.
This is the longest ruler in my pencil case.
sections.note: Do not double w, x or y. For shy in this Lab, keep y: shyer/shyest.

sections.title: Longer words and two forms
sections.text: Longer adjectives usually use more/most. The four two-syllable words listed here allow both patterns. Both forms are correct; this does not mean every two-syllable adjective can take -er/-est.
examples: This story is more interesting than the last one.
Our library is the quietest room in school.

sections.title: Irregular forms
sections.text: Some words change their forms. Do not add regular endings. For distance, both farther/farthest and further/furthest are correct.
examples: My new drawing is better than my old one.
This shop is the farthest from our school.
sections.note: Much and little describe amounts; many describes numbers. In these questions, the noun is already in the sentence.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.text: Choose one pattern. Do not put more before an -er form or most before an -est form. Use the special forms for good and bad.
examples: Ben is taller than his brother.
This is the easiest question in our homework.

sections.title: Build with blocks
sections.text: Choose every needed block. ×y removes the final y; -ier/-iest do not remove it automatically. For big, choose the extra g before the ending: doubling is not automatic either.
examples: Our kitchen is noisier than our bedroom.
Our kitchen is the noisiest room at home.

sections.title: Less and least
sections.text: Less expensive means cheaper. The least expensive means the cheapest in a group. Use less/least before the adjective to show a lower level.
examples: This pen is less expensive than that pen.
This is the least expensive pen in our school shop.

sections.title: Stronger and weaker comparisons
sections.text: Much, far and a lot make a comparison stronger. A bit, a little and slightly make it weaker. Put them before the comparative.
examples: My new bag is much heavier than my old bag.
This question is a little easier than the last one.

sections.title: As and not as
sections.text: Use as + the base adjective + as for equal qualities. Not as ... as means a lower level, like less ... than. Do not change the adjective's form.
examples: My ruler is as long as yours.
Our kitchen is not as quiet as our bedroom.

sections.title: Superlatives with groups
sections.text: Use one of the + a plural noun; among/of for a group; in for a place/group; and have ever + a past participle (see → seen).
examples: Ming is one of the tallest students.
Ming is the tallest among his friends.
Ming is the tallest in our class.
This is the best film I have ever seen.

sections.title: Make the comparison clear
sections.text: Make clear which items you mean. Yours can mean your bag; my sister's hair names the other hair being compared.
examples: My bag is heavier than yours.
My hair is longer than my sister's hair.
sections.note: Than can be left out when the comparison is already understood: Ming is tall, but Ben is taller. The Lab asks you to include it.

miniCheck.sentence: Our school hall is _____ our classroom.
miniCheck.explanation: Large ends in e, so add -r. Than introduces our classroom.

miniCheck.sentence: Of three bags, our red bag is _____.
miniCheck.explanation: Good changes to best for a group of three. Use the best in this sentence.

miniCheck.sentence: This is _____ place in our library.
miniCheck.explanation: Quiet adds -est here. The most quiet is also correct, but it is not an option.
